title: 05. Load Balancing & Scalability: What is Load Balancer?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A load balancer is a network device or software service that distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers so that no single node becomes a bottleneck — improving availability, scalability, performance, and resilience against failures.

A load balancer sits between clients and a pool of identical backend servers, acting as the single point of contact for inbound connections and then deciding, per request or per connection, which backend should handle it. The motivation is brutally simple: **one server, no matter how powerful, has a finite request capacity**. A modern web box might serve 10,000 requests per second before its CPU saturates, but a global product like Netflix serves millions of concurrent streams. The only way to bridge that gap is horizontal scaling — add more boxes — and the load balancer is the traffic cop that makes a fleet of boxes behave like one logical service to the outside world. Netflix's edge tier, for example, terminates hundreds of millions of TLS connections per day through a layer of NGINX load balancers that fan traffic out to thousands of playback-service instances across multiple AWS regions.

The **first** reason load balancers exist is **availability**. Without one, you point DNS at a single IP, and if that machine dies, your product is down until you re-provision and DNS propagates — easily hours of downtime. With a load balancer in front, you register N backends behind a virtual IP (VIP); if one dies, the load balancer detects it via health checks within seconds and stops sending traffic, while the rest of the fleet continues serving. This is the foundation of high-availability architectures: AWS ELB, Google Cloud Load Balancing, and Azure Load Balancer all use this pattern, and they typically advertise 99.99%+ availability SLAs precisely because they can route around failed instances automatically. Amazon's retail site uses Elastic Load Balancers in front of every microservice so that a single EC2 instance crash — which happens routinely across their millions of servers — never reaches a customer.

The **second** reason is **scalability**. Adding capacity to a load-balanced service is a CRUD operation: register a new backend with the balancer, and within seconds it starts receiving traffic proportional to its weight. Removing capacity is the inverse — drain the instance by setting its weight to zero, wait for in-flight requests to finish, then decommission. This elasticity is what lets Uber handle the surge from a typical Tuesday evening to a New Year's Eve peak without pre-provisioning year-round capacity. Kubernetes operationalizes this with its `Service` and `Endpoints` objects: a Service gets a stable ClusterIP, kube-proxy load-balances across the matching Pod endpoints, and the cluster can scale Pods up or down via Horizontal Pod Autoscaler without any client ever noticing. Horizontal Pod Autoscalers and Cloud Load Balancers work in concert to add capacity in seconds when CPU crosses 70%.

The **third** reason is **performance**. A well-designed load balancer routes each request to the backend best positioned to serve it quickly — the one with the lowest latency, the fewest in-flight requests, or the one geographically closest to the caller. Latency-based routing is what makes global Anycast DNS services like Cloudflare and AWS Route 53 latency-aware: a user in Tokyo hits the Singapore edge, a user in Berlin hits the Frankfurt edge, and neither traverses the trans-oceanic link. Within a single region, least-connections routing ensures that a slow backend (one running a long GC pause) does not accumulate a queue while fast backends sit idle. The performance gain is not just lower average latency — it is lower tail latency, because the worst-case request no longer lands on the worst-case server.

Load balancers come in two broad families. **Hardware load balancers** — F5 BIG-IP, Citrix NetScaler, Cisco ACE — were the enterprise default for two decades: purpose-built ASICs terminating millions of connections per second, with magical failover between redundant appliances. They are fast, expensive ($50k–$500k each), and slow to reconfigure. **Software load balancers** — NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik, AWS ELB/ALB/NLB, Google's Maglev — run on commodity hardware, are configured via YAML or API, and scale horizontally themselves. The industry has overwhelmingly moved to software: Netflix runs NGINX on EC2, Airbnb runs HAProxy, and even Google's internal Maglev is a software packet processor running on standard Linux servers, handling tens of millions of packets per second. The reason is operational: software LBs integrate with infrastructure-as-code, can be versioned in Git, and roll out in minutes rather than the months-long procurement cycles of hardware appliances.

The **core algorithms** a load balancer can use to choose a backend fall into a few families. **Round-robin** rotates sequentially through backends, assuming they are equal-capacity. **Weighted round-robin** lets you give beefier boxes more share. **Least-connections** picks the backend with the fewest active requests — the right default for variable-length requests like video transcodes. **IP-hash** (or consistent hashing) pins a client to a backend for session affinity, useful when a backend holds per-user in-memory state. **Latency-based** (sometimes called "peak EWMA") routes around slow backends automatically, popularized by the Finagle and Twitter-server stacks. Each algorithm has its phase-5 file; the choice is rarely "best" in isolation, it depends on whether backends are equal, whether sessions are sticky, and whether latency variance is high.

**Health checks** are the other half of the equation. A load balancer that routes to dead backends is worse than no load balancer at all — it actively sends traffic into a black hole. Every production LB periodically pings each backend (HTTP `GET /healthz`, TCP connect, or a custom script) and removes failing backends from the rotation. The check frequency and threshold matter: too aggressive, and a momentary GC pause will flap the backend in and out; too relaxed, and a dead instance keeps receiving traffic for minutes. AWS ALB defaults to a 30-second interval with a healthy threshold of 5 consecutive successes and an unhealthy threshold of 2 failures — meaning a hard crash is detected within 60–90 seconds. Netflix pushes further with active-active multi-region failover driven by their Eureka service registry, where backends self-register and de-register, and the Zuul gateway follows.

The trade-off is operational complexity. A load balancer is itself a distributed system that must be highly available — which is why cloud providers run them in redundant pairs with VIP failover (VRRP/keepalived), and why Netflix runs multiple Zuul instances behind AWS NLB. The balancer is a new SPOF if not designed correctly, a new bottleneck if undersized, and a new debugging surface when requests mysteriously route to the wrong place. But the upside — availability measured in nines, capacity that grows linearly with the fleet, and graceful degradation under failure — is so foundational that no production system above toy scale runs without one.

DRAINED"] LB -->|RR / LC / hash| B1 LB -->|RR / LC / hash| B2 LB -.->|"skipped (unhealthy)"| B3 B1 --> App1["App logic"] B2 --> App2["App logic"] App1 --> DB[("Database")] App2 --> DB Algorithms["Algorithms"] Algorithms --> RR["Round Robin"] Algorithms --> WRR["Weighted RR"] Algorithms --> LC["Least Connections"] Algorithms --> IPH["IP-Hash / Consistent"] Algorithms --> LAT["Latency (EWMA)"] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------+ | Clients | | (many) | +-----+-----+ | v +-----------------------+ | DNS -> VIP | +-----------+-----------+ | v +-----------------------------+ | LOAD BALANCER | <-- single entry point | (NGINX / AWS ALB / Envoy) | routes per algorithm +--+--+--+--+--+--+--+-------+ health | | | | | | | | checks v v v v v v v v +----+--+--+--+--+--+--+--+--+ | B1 | B2 | B3 | B4 | B5 | B6 | | OK | OK | OK | OK | BAD| OK | +----+----+----+----+----+----+ ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ | | | | | +----+----+----+---------+ traffic only goes to healthy backends; B5 is drained Algorithm cheatsheet: Round Robin : B1 -> B2 -> B3 -> B4 -> B6 -> B1 ... Weighted RR : B1 (w=3) -> B2 (w=2) -> B3 (w=1) ... Least Connections : pick backend with fewest in-flight reqs IP-Hash : hash(client_ip) % N -> sticky backend Latency (EWMA) : pick backend with lowest p99 latency ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Clients resolve the service hostname via DNS and receive a Virtual IP (VIP) that points at the load balancer — never directly at a backend. 2. The load balancer accepts the connection, consults its configured algorithm (round-robin, least-connections, etc.), and forwards the request to a healthy backend. 3. In parallel, the health-checker polls every backend on a fixed interval (commonly 5–30 seconds) using HTTP, TCP, or a custom probe; failures mark the backend unhealthy and remove it from rotation. 4. The chosen backend processes the request and returns the response through the load balancer (or directly to the client, in DSR mode) — from the client's perspective, the entire fleet looks like one server. 5. When capacity changes — autoscaler adds a box, or an instance is drained for deploy — the backend list updates and the balancer's algorithm rebalances traffic within seconds, with no client-side awareness.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Abstract base class for a Load Balancer with health checks and backends.
# Demonstrates the core ideas: backend pool, health check loop, pluggable
# selection algorithm. Subclasses (RoundRobin, LeastConnections, ...) override
# `pick_backend()`.

import threading
import time
import random
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Backend:
    """A single backend server behind the load balancer."""
    address: str               # e.g. "10.0.1.5:8080"
    weight: int = 1            # used by weighted algorithms
    healthy: bool = True       # set by the health checker
    in_flight: int = 0         # used by least-connections
    last_check: float = 0.0    # epoch seconds of last health probe
    _lock: threading.Lock = field(default_factory=threading.Lock)

    def mark(self, ok: bool):
        with self._lock:
            self.healthy = ok
            self.last_check = time.time()

class LoadBalancer(ABC):
    """Abstract load balancer: owns backends + health checks + selection."""

    def __init__(self, backends: list[Backend], check_interval: float = 10.0):
        self.backends = backends
        self.check_interval = check_interval
        self._stop = threading.Event()
        self._hc_thread = threading.Thread(target=self._health_loop, daemon=True)

    # ----- subclass implements the selection algorithm -----
    @abstractmethod
    def pick_backend(self) -> Backend | None:
        ...

    # ----- health checking: every backend pinged on a timer -----
    def _health_loop(self):
        while not self._stop.is_set():
            for b in self.backends:
                ok = self._probe(b)
                was_healthy = b.healthy
                b.mark(ok)
                if was_healthy and not ok:
                    print(f"[HC] {b.address} went UNHEALTHY -- draining")
                if not was_healthy and ok:
                    print(f"[HC] {b.address} recovered -- re-adding")
            self._stop.wait(self.check_interval)

    def _probe(self, b: Backend) -> bool:
        # In real life: TCP connect or HTTP GET /healthz.
        # Mock: 2% chance of failure to simulate transient flaps.
        return random.random() > 0.02

    # ----- public API used by the request handler -----
    def handle_request(self, req_id: int):
        b = self.pick_backend()
        if b is None:
            print(f"[LB] req {req_id} -> 503 (no healthy backends)")
            return
        with b._lock:
            b.in_flight += 1
        try:
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0.005, 0.02))  # mock work
            print(f"[LB] req {req_id} -> {b.address}")
        finally:
            with b._lock:
                b.in_flight -= 1

    def start(self): self._hc_thread.start()
    def stop(self):  self._stop.set(); self._hc_thread.join(timeout=2)

class RoundRobinLB(LoadBalancer):
    """Naive round-robin: rotate through healthy backends."""
    def __init__(self, backends, check_interval=10.0):
        super().__init__(backends, check_interval)
        self._idx = 0
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def pick_backend(self):
        healthy = [b for b in self.backends if b.healthy]
        if not healthy:
            return None
        with self._lock:
            b = healthy[self._idx % len(healthy)]
            self._idx += 1
        return b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    backends = [Backend(f"10.0.1.{i}:8080", weight=1) for i in range(1, 5)]
    lb = RoundRobinLB(backends, check_interval=3.0)
    lb.start()
    for i in range(10):
        lb.handle_request(i)
    lb.stop()
```

quiz.explanation: A load balancer solves three problems at once: availability (one server dying should not take the product down), scalability (capacity should grow with the fleet, not with the box), and performance (requests should land on the fastest or least-loaded backend).

quiz.explanation: Hardware load balancers (F5 BIG-IP, Citrix NetScaler) are purpose-built appliances with custom ASICs that terminate millions of connections per second, sold as physical boxes with a fixed capacity and a months-long procurement cycle. Software load balancers (NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, AWS ELB) run on commodity servers or as managed cloud services, configured via YAML or API, and can be deployed in minutes.
